title: The verb that must sit in second place
title_target: I dag går jeg på universitetet
goal: Master the single most decisive rule in all of Norwegian grammar: whatever stands at the start of the sentence, the verb stays in second place.
bekal: build sentences that start with a time expression without breaking the word order
recognize a dozen opening words that push the subject behind the verb
read long sentences using a five-slot frame
wave: Go back over **Unit 1** first: cover the Norwegian, look at the English translation, and rebuild the dialogue from memory. Notice how many verb forms you have to learn — the answer is still one per verb.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Mandag morgen
dialogs.intro: Monday morning, just after seven. It's still dark outside. Ingrid finds Budi standing, puzzled, by the front door.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: God morgen! Hva gjør du i dag?
lines.id: Good morning! What are you doing today?
lines.literal: good morning! what do you in day?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: I dag går jeg på universitetet.
lines.id: Today I'm going to the university.
lines.literal: in day go I on the-university.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Klokka ni. Derfor står jeg opp så tidlig.
lines.id: At nine. That's why I get up so early.
lines.literal: the-clock nine. therefore stand I up so early.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Om vinteren er det mørkt klokka ni.
lines.id: In winter it's dark at nine.
lines.literal: in the-winter is it dark the-clock nine.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Det forstår jeg ikke. Hjemme er det lyst klokka seks.
lines.id: That I don't understand. At home it's light at six.
lines.literal: that understand I not. at-home is it light the-clock six.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Etter timen drikker vi kaffe sammen?
lines.id: After class, shall we have coffee together?
lines.literal: after the-hour drink we coffee together?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Gjerne! Men i morgen jobber jeg.
lines.id: I'd love to! But tomorrow I'm working.
lines.literal: gladly! but in morning work I.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Da tar vi det i dag.
lines.literal: then take we it in day.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Perfekt. Nå må jeg løpe — bussen går om fem minutter!
lines.id: Perfect. Now I have to run — the bus leaves in five minutes!
lines.literal: perfect. now must I run — the-bus goes in five minutes!

notes: **This is the unit that shapes the whole course.** Read line two again: *I dag **går jeg*** — not *i dag jeg går*. As soon as something stands at the front of the sentence, the verb stays in second place and **the subject jumps behind it**. This is called the V2 rule, and it applies without exception in every main clause.

**English has almost lost this rule.** "Today I'm going" and "I'm going today" are both fine, and the subject always comes before the verb. Only fossils like "Here comes the bus" or "Never have I seen…" remain. So in the first month an English speaker's hand almost always writes *i dag jeg går* — and a Norwegian immediately hears it as a broken sentence.

**Derfor står jeg opp** — the word *derfor* ("therefore, that's why") also fills the first slot, so *står* stays second and *jeg* moves back. The same pattern holds for *da*, *nå*, *så*, *kanskje*, *heldigvis* and every time expression.

**Det forstår jeg ikke** shows that the first slot doesn't have to be an adverb — it can also be the **object**. Literally "that understand I not". This order is used for emphasis: whatever you move to the front is what you want to highlight.

**Gjerne** is pronounced **YÆR-neh**. The combination *gj-* always sounds like *y*, just like *hj-*: *gjøre* → **YÖ-reh**, *hjelpe* → **YEL-peh**. It means "gladly" and is the standard answer to an offer.

**Å stå opp** (to get up out of bed) is a phrasal verb: *opp* sticks to it and changes its meaning, just like English *get up*, *go out* or *switch on* (*å gå ut*, *å slå på*). The particle stands at the back, after the subject when the sentence is inverted: *står **jeg** opp*.

grammars.title: The Norwegian sentence frame
body: Picture every Norwegian sentence as five boxes in a row. The second box **always** holds the present-tense verb. The first box can hold anything — and whatever you put there, the second box doesn't move.
after: Look at the first row: when the subject itself fills the first box, the third box is empty. That's the ordinary sentence that feels most "normal" — and that's exactly why beginners forget it's only **one of several possibilities**.
The last row shows a yes/no question: the first box is completely empty, so the verb ends up in front. Same rule, not a new one.
If you're unsure whether a sentence is right, just count: **what position is the verb in?** If it isn't second, something's wrong.

grammars.title: Openers that force inversion
body: All of the following words and phrases, when they stand at the start of a sentence, push the subject behind the verb. The list is short and worth learning whole.
after: ⚠️ Two words that **don't** force inversion, because they only join two equal sentences and don't fill the first box: **og** (and) and **men** (but). *Jeg jobber, **men jeg** går på universitetet i morgen* — here *jeg* stays in front of the verb. Other linking words such as *for* (because) and *eller* (or) work the same way.
How to test it: if you can cut the sentence at that word and both pieces stand on their own as complete sentences, the word is a linker, not an opener.

sections.title: Eye training: one sentence, four openers

blocks.text: Read each row aloud from left to right. The content is exactly the same; only what stands in front changes. This drill looks boring, and it's precisely the one that gets the rule into your hand fastest.
Look at the last column: *ikke* loyally follows the verb + subject pair, wherever that pair is. And in the last row, the particle *opp* gets thrown right to the end — after *ikke*.

sections.title: Why English speakers almost always stumble here

blocks.text: English builds sentences on a fixed **subject–verb** core: whatever you put in front — "Tomorrow", "In Bergen", "That's why" — the subject still comes before the verb. "Tomorrow I'm going to Bergen" feels perfectly natural. That habit feels normal until you carry it into Norwegian, where there's one slot that nothing but the verb may fill.

items: **Most common mistake:** writing *I morgen jeg kommer*. The right form is *I morgen **kommer jeg***. If you're unsure, say it slowly and count on your fingers: one — *i morgen*, two — *kommer*.
**Second mistake:** dragging *ikke* to the front as well. *I dag ikke jobber jeg* is wrong twice over. The right form is *I dag jobber jeg ikke*.
**Third mistake:** assuming *og* and *men* also force inversion. *Jeg er trøtt, men går jeg likevel* is wrong — the right form is *men **jeg går** likevel*.

blocks.title: A quick self-test
items: Write five sentences about today, all starting with the subject. Then rewrite all five starting with a time expression. If even one of them keeps the same order in the second version, go over this page again.
The V2 rule also applies in German, Dutch, Swedish and Danish. Once you've got it, you've got it for five languages at once.

What does **not** follow V2 is the subordinate clause — the piece starting with *at*, *fordi*, *hvis*, *når*. There the order is different and *ikke* moves in front of the verb. That's for Unit 18; leave it alone for now.
